title: Bell and House
premise: Jude Pemberton takes a teaching post in the fog-bound town of Hollowmere, where a classroom of children vanished decades ago and the town has agreed, collectively, to forget. Jude's rented house—the old Bell residence—begins reflecting rooms one second behind, and in that stolen second Jude glimpses the missing class still at their desks, singing a song that erases whoever learns its final verse. As Jude uncovers that their own childhood silence made them a vessel the house has been waiting to fill, they must choose between joining the found family trapped inside the mirrors or breaking the song by teaching it a new last verse—one written from memory and love rather than loss. In the end Jude sings the changed verse aloud, freeing the children into forgetting and claiming, for the first time, a belonging that doesn't require disappearing.
about_author: Orsen Halloran is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent eleven years in coastal towns where the fog arrives earlier than the school bus. They write horror about quiet people and the houses that notice them, and they still refuse to sing in front of mirrors.

chapters.title: The Position Is Still Open
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Jude Pemberton, who arrives in Hollowmere to teach the combined class no one else will take. The headmistress mentions, too casually, that Room 4 has been 'between cohorts' since 1984. Jude, practiced at being unremarkable, unpacks in a rented house called Bell House. Emotional beat: cautious hope shadowed by the ache of always being new.

chapters.title: Twenty-Three Desks
chapters.summary: Jude counts twenty-three desks in a classroom with eleven enrolled students; the extra twelve are worn smooth as river stones. A custodian named Wren tells them not to move anything after dark. Jude's POV stays close and rationalizing—they catalog explanations like a hobby. Emotional beat: the comfort of rationality beginning to feel like a performance.

chapters.title: What the Fog Keeps
chapters.summary: Walking home through fog that arrives before dusk, Jude hears children singing a round with no final verse—it simply stops, mid-phrase. Their landlady, Mrs. Aldous, hums along without realizing, then goes pale when Jude names the tune. Third-person limited, Jude. Emotional beat: first crack in the armor of explanation.

chapters.title: Bell House, One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Alone at night, Jude notices the hallway mirror showing them turning their head a beat late—then catching up. Every reflective surface in the house does it: windows, kettle, the dark TV screen. Jude tests it with a metronome app until the app itself lags. POV Jude. Emotional beat: terror braided with a shameful thrill at finally being noticed by something.

chapters.title: The Class Photo That Isn't
chapters.summary: In the school archive Jude finds the 1984 class photo: twelve smiling children, faces smudged as if breathed-on glass. The archivist insists there was never a photo. Wren quietly slips Jude a duplicate negative and says, 'They were good kids. Loud ones.' POV Jude. Emotional beat: grief for strangers, and the suspicion that forgetting here is a choice the town keeps making.

chapters.title: Reflections Take Attendance
chapters.summary: The lag grows to two seconds. In the mirror, Jude's kitchen shows twelve small figures seated at the table, hands folded, waiting. When Jude speaks to them, the glass ripples like struck water. Mrs. Aldous stops answering her door. POV Jude. Emotional beat: loneliness curdling into complicity—Jude realizes part of them wants to sit down.

chapters.title: Wren's Confession
chapters.summary: Wren, the custodian, was the teacher who survived 1984. Over cheap whisky he explains: the song is a door, the house a throat, and the verse everyone refuses to learn is the one that closes it. He learned all but the last line and has hummed around it for forty years. POV shifts briefly to Wren. Emotional beat: survivor's guilt offered like a warning label.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Jude begins transcribing the song from mirror-memory, writing notes they must never voice. Each verse learned makes the reflections clearer—and makes Jude's own reflection start arriving early instead of late. The house is learning them back. POV Jude. Emotional beat: the vertigo of studying something that studies you harder.

chapters.title: The Children Know My Name
chapters.summary: A student, Ilsa Vane, draws Jude's face surrounded by twelve others and says, 'They said you'd come. They've been saving your seat.' Jude reports it; the headmistress's office contains only dust and a bell rope. POV Jude. Emotional beat: protectiveness igniting—Jude's invisibility ends the moment someone else is at risk.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Sings
chapters.summary: Jude finds their landlady standing before her bathroom mirror, singing the round fluently, eyes bright and empty. Her flat is already reflected empty behind her. Jude drags her out by the arm; she doesn't recognize the house she's lived in for fifty years. POV Jude. Emotional beat: horror sharpened into urgency—the song takes the lonely first.

chapters.title: The Town That Agreed
chapters.summary: At the pub, Jude confronts the town's collective amnesia; the bartender's smile doesn't waver as he explains that remembering invites the house to expand. Old newspaper clippings burn in the hearth before Jude can read them. POV Jude. Emotional beat: fury at a community that bought safety with its own children.

chapters.title: Verse Eleven
chapters.summary: Transcribing alone, Jude reaches the eleventh verse and understands the structure: each verse is a memory surrendered. The twelfth—the last—must be the singer's own dearest memory, given willingly. The house has been starving because Jude has never had one worth taking. POV Jude. Emotional beat: devastating self-recognition beneath the dread.

chapters.title: Ilsa Follows the Sound
chapters.summary: Isla goes missing after school; her boots are found outside Bell House, toes pointed at the door. Inside, the mirrors show her seated among the twelve, holding a hymnal. Wren says the house only opens its throat for those who belong to it—and now Jude does. POV Jude. Emotional beat: guilt transformed into resolve.

chapters.title: Entering the Second
chapters.summary: Jude presses their palm to the lagging mirror during the stolen second and steps through into Bell House's interior: an endless schoolroom lit by fog-colored windows, where thirteen children wait and time moves like syrup. POV Jude, disoriented second-person interludes. Emotional beat: awe and wrongness—the found family that shouldn't exist feels almost like home.

chapters.title: The Twelve
chapters.summary: Among the children, Jude meets the class of 1984: they remember everything, which is why they can't leave. Their teacher-figure, a woman made partly of doorway, explains the house keeps what sings and starves without a final verse. They don't want rescue; they want an ending. POV alternates Jude and the eldest child, Merrin. Emotional beat: compassion replacing fear.

chapters.title: What Jude Buried
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: young Jude, passed between foster homes, learned that being forgettable kept them safe—the noises in every temporary house were easier to explain than to answer. The present-day house offers to take that nothingness as the final verse. POV Jude, past tense bleeding into present. Emotional beat: the theme crystallizes—invisibility was survival, but it was never living.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The house speaks through every mirror at once: sing the true last verse—your emptiest memory—and stay forever, wanted, among the twelve, with Ilsa freed. It shows Jude a warm imagined life inside the glass. Wren's voice reaches faintly through, humming the eleven verses as a lifeline. POV Jude. Emotional beat: temptation rendered genuinely kind, which makes it monstrous.

chapters.title: Writing the Twelfth Verse
chapters.summary: Instead of surrendering a memory, Jude writes a new final verse on the classroom chalkboard—a verse about staying, about choosing people in daylight, built from the small real moments of the past weeks. The children lean in. The house shudders; songs can be rewritten if the singer means it. POV Jude. Emotional beat: defiant tenderness as the weapon.

chapters.title: Sung Aloud
chapters.summary: Climax. Jude sings the rewritten verse fully, voice cracking, while the house tries to drown them in fog and remembered silence. The twelve join on the new ending; the doorway-woman smiles and comes apart into morning light. Ilsa wakes on the doorstep. The mirrors go perfectly, boringly, exactly on time. POV Jude. Emotional beat: catharsis—being heard for the first time.

chapters.title: Aftermath in Daylight
chapters.summary: The town remembers all at once—grief arriving like weather. Funerals without bodies; the headmistress resigns; Wren weeps over forty years of humming. Jude stays, refusing the transfer, and teaches in Room 4 with twenty-three desks, twelve of them now just furniture. POV Jude. Emotional beat: sorrow and settlement entwined.

chapters.title: Found Family, Found Verse
chapters.summary: Weeks later: Ilsa eats dinner at Bell House, Wren fixes the porch step, and the town slowly learns to say the children's names again. Jude catches their reflection keeping perfect time and, for once, waves at it. The house is only a house—but a hospitable one. POV Jude. Emotional beat: belonging earned rather than haunted into place.

chapters.title: Coda: The Song Continues
chapters.summary: Final chapter: on the last day of term, Jude teaches the class a new round—with a proper ending this time—and the children carry it out into the fog, loud and off-key. Somewhere deep in the walls, something old listens, finds nothing left to take, and settles. Last image: a mirror, one second early, just once, as if waving goodbye. POV Jude. Emotional beat: peace with a pulse of wonder.
